title: The World the Mongols Broke
bullets: Russia begins with a funeral, not a founding: when the story opens in the winter of 1237 there is no Russia, only the wreckage the Mongols are about to make of Kievan Rus'.

The Mongols rode out of the Eurasian steppe under the sons of Genghis Khan, an almost all-cavalry war machine that built the largest contiguous land empire in history with siege engineers, a postal relay, and a surrender-or-be-annihilated policy.

Russians called the invaders Tatars, not Mongols, and this book uses that word throughout, because the Mongol-led power was Mongol at the top and Turkic in the mass of its people and the sources blur the two.

Batu Khan campaigned in winter, when the Rus' rivers and swamps froze into hard roads a cavalry army could ride straight down; the cold that should have protected the forest cities instead paved the way to them.
Vladimir was stormed and burned in February 1238 and Grand Prince Yuri II was killed with his army at the Sit River, beheading the political order of the northeast in a single campaign season.

Batu returned in 1240 and gutted Kiev; the friar Giovanni da Pian del Carpine passed through six years later and found the ground still littered with skulls and a great metropolis shrunk to a couple hundred houses.
The catastrophe shifted Russia's center of gravity north and east into the cold, poor, river-veined taiga forest around Vladimir, Suzdal, Tver, and an utterly obscure little town called Moscow.
The one institution that bridged the old world and the new was the Orthodox Church, which the Mongols had no interest in destroying and which alone still spanned all the Rus' lands.

The sources are a problem from the start: the chronicles (letopisi) were written for princes and monasteries and edited the past to make the present look inevitable, so a careful reader asks who paid for each page.

title: Living Under the Yoke
bullets: The Tatar yoke was not an occupation but a protection racket run on a continental scale: the Mongols left the Rus' princes on their thrones and simply skimmed wealth and obedience from a distance through threat and paperwork.

The Golden Horde was Batu's permanent state on the lower Volga, ruled from the cosmopolitan trading city of Sarai, increasingly Turkic and eventually Muslim, with the Rus' princes as its tribute-paying tributaries.

Three instruments ran the racket: the census of 1257 that counted every household for the tax rolls, the tribute paid in silver, and the yarlyk, the khan's written patent without which no prince could legitimately rule.

The yarlyk made princes travel to Sarai to flatter, bribe, and outmaneuver their rivals for the khan's favor, and the competition was deadly: princes denounced and executed each other at the foreign court.
Alexander Nevsky beat the Swedes at the Neva in 1240 and the Teutonic Knights on the frozen Lake Peipus in 1242 at the Battle on the Ice, checking the Catholic crusading push from the west.

Then Nevsky turned around and submitted to the Mongols, paying tribute and even enforcing the hated census against his own Novgorod, on the cold logic that the East could be appeased with silver while the West wanted your soul.

In 1267 the Horde exempted the Orthodox Church from tribute and service, so while princes and peasants were squeezed for silver the Church grew rich, becoming the wealthiest and most stable institution in the land.
How heavy the yoke really was is a genuine debate: the Mongol presence was light after the conquest, and the claim that Mongols invented Russian autocracy is now treated with deep suspicion.

title: The Rise of the Moneybag
bullets: Moscow rose not because God chose it, as the Moscow chronicles claim, but because its princes were the most reliable, ruthless, and useful servants the Mongol khan had in a world run as a protection racket.

In 1283 the swampy little town on the Moskva River was given as an appanage to Daniel, youngest son of Alexander Nevsky, who founded the line and began the relentless land-grabbing later called the gathering of the Russian lands.

For the first half of the fourteenth century Moscow's central rival was Tver, a stronger, older, richer principality upstream on the Volga, and their feud was fought at Sarai with gifts, slander, and executions rather than on the battlefield.

Ivan I, nicknamed Kalita or Moneybag, became the Horde's bagman by winning the right to collect everyone's tribute, then skimming it, timing it, and converting the silver that passed through his hands into land and leverage.

In 1327 the people of Tver rose and killed a Mongol envoy, and Ivan Kalita rode to Sarai and personally led a Mongol army back to devastate his chief Russian rival, an act of breathtaking collaboration that worked perfectly.

Around 1325 the Metropolitan Peter chose to live and be buried in Moscow, and from about 1328 the spiritual capital of the Russian lands was the same town as its rising political capital, marrying throne to altar.

The Black Death reached the Russian lands by about 1352 and in 1353 killed Grand Prince Simeon the Proud and his sons in a single sweep, binding Russia into the one shared catastrophe of the fourteenth-century world.
Around 1345 Sergius of Radonezh withdrew into the forest and founded the Trinity Monastery, sparking a monastic revival whose disciples colonized the wilderness and sanctified Moscow's cause.

title: Kulikovo and the Idea of Resistance
bullets: A prince of Moscow finally stopped paying the tribute and won a battle against the Mongols that Russians remembered for six hundred years, though it mattered far more as a story than as a fact.

Dmitry Ivanovich, grandson of Ivan Kalita, replaced Moscow's oak walls in 1367 with white limestone, the first stone fortress in the northeastern lands and the origin of the Kremlin and the city's name as the white-stone city.

Open defiance became thinkable because the Horde had fallen into a long internal crisis, the great troubles, and power had passed to the strongman Mamai, who was not of Genghis Khan's blood and so could not legitimately be khan.
Dmitry crushed a Mongol force at the Vozha River in 1378, the first significant Russian victory over a Horde army in the open field, proving the unthinkable that the Tatars could be beaten.

At the Battle of Kulikovo near the Don on September 8, 1380, Dmitry defeated Mamai and earned the name Dmitry Donskoy, but the famous details of monks, single combat, and an ambush regiment come from later epics like the Zadonshchina.

Kulikovo did not end the yoke: just two years later Tokhtamysh, a prince of the genuine Genghisid line, sacked and burned Moscow in 1382, the tribute resumed, and Dmitry sent his own son to Sarai as a hostage.

Kulikovo changed the story rather than the facts, giving Russians proof that the yoke was not eternal and that Moscow was the sword of Orthodox Russia, a founding national myth whose legend outran the reality by a century.

Around 1378 Theophanes the Greek brought late-Byzantine fresco painting to Novgorod and Moscow, and a generation later the monk Andrei Rublev painted the Trinity icon, the summit of Russian medieval art.

As late as 1408 the Horde commander Edigu could still ravage the Moscow lands and besiege the city, while Dmitry's son Vasily I kept gathering land by buying a yarlyk for Nizhny Novgorod from the khan.

title: The Gathering of the Lands
bullets: Vasily I simply bought the rival principality of Nizhny Novgorod in 1392 by purchasing a yarlyk for it from the khan, the land-gathering in its purest, least romantic form: a real-estate deal backed by a foreign emperor's stamp.

In 1395 the Central Asian conqueror Timur, known as Tamerlane, fell on the Golden Horde and wrecked it, a wound from outside it never recovered from, and the once-unified Horde began splintering into Kazan, Astrakhan, Crimea, and the Great Horde.

When Vasily I died in 1425 the throne was disputed under the old lateral succession rule, brother to brother, touching off the roughly twenty-year Muscovite War of Succession fought over which inheritance rule Moscow would use.
The war was waged with blindings: Vasily II's faction blinded his cousin Vasily Kosoy, and in 1446 the other side captured Vasily II and put out his eyes, leaving him known as Vasily the Blind.

Vasily the Blind won anyway, clawing back from captivity, and in winning fixed father-to-son primogeniture forever, the unglamorous rule that made Moscow's monarchy uniquely stable while rivals tore themselves apart.

At the Council of Florence in 1439 the desperate Byzantines signed a union accepting the pope's authority, and Moscow's Greek metropolitan Isidore came home a cardinal proclaiming it and was arrested as a heretic.

In 1448 the Russian bishops elected their own metropolitan Jonah without asking Constantinople, making the Russian Church effectively autocephalous, self-headed, with no master abroad for the first time.

When the Ottoman Turks took Constantinople in 1453, Moscow read it as God punishing the Greeks for the Florentine betrayal, leaving Moscow the only major independent Orthodox power and seeding the Third Rome idea.

title: Ivan the Great and the Third Rome
bullets: Ivan III took the throne in 1462 without a fight and over forty-three years did more to create Russia than any ruler before him, dying as sovereign of a unified state three times the size, answerable to no one.

In 1478 Ivan crushed and annexed Novgorod, Russia's only real tradition of self-government through its citizen assembly the veche, and carted the veche bell away to Moscow, silencing the republican idea along with the city.

In 1472 Ivan married Sophia Palaiologina, niece of the last Byzantine emperor, claiming the imperial inheritance of fallen Byzantium, and the double-headed eagle began appearing on his seals and became Russia's coat of arms.

The Great Stand on the Ugra River in 1480 ended more than two centuries of Mongol overlordship without a battle: the two armies sat glaring across the water for weeks, then both simply turned around and went home.

Ivan rebuilt the Kremlin with Italian engineers, the best in Europe at fortification: Aristotele Fioravanti built the Dormition Cathedral in 1479 and Italians raised the red brick walls that look so quintessentially Russian.

The 1497 Sudebnik, the first law code of the centralized state, restricted peasants to leaving their lord only during a two-week window around St. George's Day, the first legal crack in the door toward full serfdom.

Around 1510 the monk Philotheus of Pskov wrote that Moscow was the third Rome and a fourth there would never be, a couple of lines in a letter urging piety, not the imperial doctrine later writers inflated it into.

Modern historians are skeptical that the Third Rome ever functioned as a state doctrine; it was rediscovered and exaggerated in the 1800s and 1900s by writers hunting a deep explanation for Russia's ambitions.

title: The First Tsar
bullets: Vasily III spent his reign tidying up, annexing Pskov in 1510, Smolensk from Lithuania in 1514, and Ryazan, so that by the 1520s the gathering of the Great Russian lands was essentially complete.

Vasily died in 1533 leaving a three-year-old heir, Ivan IV, and a chaotic regency in which the great boyar families plotted, murdered, and looted in the boy's name, the trauma later chroniclers blamed for the monster he became.

In 1547, at sixteen, Ivan IV was crowned not grand prince but Tsar of All Rus', the first ruler to take the title formally, claiming to be an emperor of the same rank as the Caesars of Rome and Constantinople.

In the good years Ivan governed with the Chosen Council, summoning the first Zemsky Sobor or assembly of the land in 1549, issuing a new Sudebnik in 1550, and creating the streltsy, Russia's first permanent firearm-equipped infantry.

The 1551 church council the Stoglav froze Russian ritual exactly as it stood, a time bomb that guaranteed a later attempt to correct those rites would feel like an attack on the holy and split the Church.

Ivan stormed Kazan in 1552 and took Astrakhan in 1556, two Muslim Tatar khanates on the Volga, giving Russia the entire length of the river and reversing three centuries of Russian humiliation before the steppe.

Conquering Kazan and Astrakhan made Russia for the first time a multi-ethnic, multi-faith empire ruling Muslims and Turkic and Finno-Ugric peoples, the hinge on which Russia stops being a nation and starts becoming an empire.

To celebrate Kazan, Ivan raised Saint Basil's Cathedral on Red Square around 1561, a riotous cluster of nine differently colored onion domes, a thoroughly Russian explosion of color with no European model.

In 1553 Richard Chancellor's English expedition blundered onto the White Sea coast, opening the first direct trade link with Western Europe through the Muscovy Company, and in 1564 Ivan Fyodorov printed Russia's first dated book.

title: The Terror
bullets: The same Ivan IV who built Saint Basil's became Grozny, the Terrible, a word closer to awe-inspiring or dread, turning the machinery of the state against his own people in a terror historians still argue about.

Two losses around 1560 began the descent: the death of his wife Anastasia Romanovna, which he came to believe was murder by the boyars, and the launch of the Livonian War in 1558, a quarter-century quagmire he could not win.

In 1564 his senior commander Prince Andrei Kurbsky defected to Lithuania and wrote the tsar a furious open letter, beginning the Ivan-Kurbsky correspondence, a real-time argument about whether a ruler is bound by anything but God.

Late in 1564 Ivan left Moscow, threatened to abdicate, and returned only when granted absolute, unlimited power to destroy traitors however he pleased, engineering a situation in which the nation begged him to become a tyrant.

The oprichnina, established in 1565, split Russia in two: a vast personal domain of perhaps a third of the country that belonged to the tsar alone, outside all law, with the old landowning families thrown off their estates.

The oprichniki, Ivan's enforcers dressed in black on black horses carrying a dog's head and a broom, were a secret police, private army, and death squad that gutted the old aristocracy from 1565 to 1572.
In 1570 Ivan fell on Novgorod on probably forged evidence of treason, massacring inhabitants for weeks and drowning people under the river ice, leaving the old city permanently broken.

The terror left Russia defenseless: the Crimean Tatars burned Moscow to the ground in 1571, before a reunited Russian army shattered them at the Battle of Molodi in 1572, after which Ivan quietly abolished the oprichnina.

In 1581 Ivan killed his own capable heir with a blow from his iron-tipped staff, leaving the throne to the feeble Fyodor and dooming the dynasty, while a Cossack band under Yermak cracked open Siberia in 1582.

title: The Dynasty Burns Out
bullets: When Ivan the Terrible died in 1584, the line of Rurik that had ruled the Russian lands for roughly seven hundred years was about to run out of men, having lost its capable heir to Ivan's own staff three years before.
The heir Fyodor I was by every account a gentle, pious, simple-minded man who liked to ring church bells, so real power fell to his brother-in-law, the gifted and much-slandered boyar Boris Godunov.

Godunov was the real government of Russia for fourteen years, stabilizing the finances Ivan had wrecked and defending the southern frontier against the Crimean Tatars who raided and enslaved their way north almost every year.

In 1589 Godunov pulled off a coup of self-regard, squeezing the visiting patriarch of Constantinople into elevating the metropolitan of Moscow to patriarch, the fifth in the Orthodox world, the rank the Third Rome demanded.

Around 1592 Godunov suspended the last St. George's Day window for peasants to leave their lords, the decisive turn toward serfdom, driven not by malice but by the need to keep the land-paid service cavalry in the saddle.

In May 1591 Ivan's youngest son, the boy Dmitry, died of a knife wound to the throat at Uglich; a commission ruled it an accident from an epileptic fit, but the verdict satisfied almost no one and never would.
Fyodor died childless in January 1598, ending the line of Rurik, and the Zemsky Sobor, managed by Godunov's allies, elected Boris Godunov tsar, the sensible choice with no obvious rival.

Godunov had broken the spell of legitimacy by taking the throne without the sacred bloodline, making the crown grabbable by anyone with an army and a story, a weakness no good government could repair.

From 1601 three years of catastrophic harvest failure, likely the global aftershock of the Huaynaputina eruption in Peru, brought the Great Famine that may have killed two million and read to a devout people as God's verdict on a false tsar.

title: The Time of Troubles
bullets: The Time of Troubles, the Smuta, was the roughly fifteen-year period in which the Russian state effectively dissolved into famine, civil war, impostors, foreign armies, and a Polish garrison inside the Moscow Kremlin.

Godunov's elective throne made the crown available to anyone, and the one thing that could trump him was a genuine heir of Rurik, so a young man surfaced in Poland claiming to be the Tsarevich Dmitry, rescued from Uglich.

The First False Dmitry, identified by the government as a defrocked monk named Grigory Otrepyev, won Polish-Lithuanian backing, secretly converted to Catholicism, and rode into Moscow to be crowned tsar in June 1605.

The pretender lasted under a year: he kept his Polish entourage, married a Polish Catholic bride in Orthodox Moscow, and a boyar conspiracy under Vasily Shuisky raised the city, killed him, and fired his ashes from a cannon toward Poland.

Shuisky grabbed the crown next with no more blood-right than Godunov, and the country no longer recognized any rule, so a vast revolt under the former military slave Ivan Bolotnikov and then a Second False Dmitry at Tushino split Russia into rival courts.

In 1609 King Sigismund III of Poland-Lithuania dropped the pretenders and invaded outright; his winged hussars annihilated a larger Russian-Swedish army at the Battle of Klushino in 1610, leaving the road to Moscow open.

At the bottom, the council of the Seven Boyars offered the throne to Sigismund's son Wladyslaw and opened the gates, letting a Polish Catholic garrison march into the Kremlin, the closest Russia ever came to disappearing.

Salvation came not from a tsar but from the Church and the towns: the imprisoned Patriarch Hermogenes smuggled out letters calling Russians to rise, and a Nizhny Novgorod butcher named Kuzma Minin raised a self-financed army.

Minin funded it and the honest prince Dmitry Pozharsky commanded it; their militia stormed Moscow in 1612 and starved out the Polish garrison, and in 1613 a great Zemsky Sobor elected the sixteen-year-old Michael Romanov tsar.

title: Rebuilding and the Great Schism
bullets: The first Romanovs inherited a ruin: when Michael was crowned in 1613, large parts of Russia were burned and depopulated, the treasury was empty, Smolensk was Polish, and the Swedes sat on the Baltic.

For the crucial early years Michael's father Filaret, made patriarch on his return from Polish captivity in 1619, was co-ruler in everything but name, using the prestige of the Church to stabilize the shattered state.

The defeat in the Smolensk War of 1632 exposed that the old gentry cavalry was hopelessly outclassed by Western infantry, so from the 1630s Russia hired foreign officers to raise drilled regiments of the new order.

Alexis, the quiet tsar who came to the throne in 1645, presided over an earthquake: the Salt Riot of 1648, the Copper Riot of 1662, total serfdom, the annexation of Ukraine, and the splitting of the Church.

The 1649 law code, the Sobornoye Ulozhenie, abolished the statute of limitations on runaway peasants and made the binding hereditary forever, completing serfdom just as Western Europe was striking the peasant's bonds off.

In 1654 at Pereyaslav the Cossack hetman Bohdan Khmelnytsky swore allegiance to Tsar Alexis, an agreement Russians and Ukrainians have read oppositely ever since and which won Russia back Smolensk and the ancient mother-city of Kiev.

From 1653 Patriarch Nikon corrected Russian rites to match the Greeks, ordering the three-fingered cross and respelling Jesus, tiny changes that to the devout meant their saintly ancestors had been damned heretics.

The resistance crystallized around the Archpriest Avvakum, burned at the stake in 1682, and the Old Believers broke away for good in 1666, with thousands burning themselves alive rather than accept the three-fingered cross.

The same 1666 council that condemned the Old Believers deposed Nikon himself for claiming the Church stood above the tsar, settling that in Russia the crown outranks the patriarch, the Church a pillar of the state and not its master.

title: The Young Peter and the End of Muscovy
bullets: The last tsar of Muscovy, Peter the Great, was almost seven feet tall, worked with his own hands in foreign shipyards, and despised nearly everything about the holy, bearded, inward-looking old Russia he was born to rule.

His accession began in blood when the Streltsy rose in May 1682 and butchered his Naryshkin relatives in front of the nine-year-old boy, ending in a bizarre double monarchy of Peter and his sickly half-brother Ivan as co-tsars.

Pushed to the margins under the regency of his half-sister Sophia, Peter built real play regiments out of stable boys and haunted Moscow's German Quarter, absorbing a conviction that the Western world of skill and the sea was the future.

In 1689 Peter faced Sophia down and forced her into a convent, then in 1695 failed to take the Ottoman fortress of Azov for lack of a navy, built a fleet in a single furious winter, and took it from the sea in 1696.

In 1697 and 1698 Peter traveled west with the Grand Embassy, working as a laborer in Dutch and English shipyards and recruiting hundreds of foreign experts, the first Russian sovereign to go west to study the West.

On his return Peter crushed a Streltsy mutiny with hundreds of public executions, then began shearing off his noblemen's beards and imposing Western dress, a beard tax, and the European calendar on a horrified, devout population.

In the Great Northern War against Sweden, Peter was routed at Narva in 1700, rebuilt his army on European lines, founded Saint Petersburg on a drowned Baltic delta in 1703, and destroyed Charles XII's Swedes at Poltava in 1709.

Peter abolished the patriarchate and replaced it with the state-run Holy Synod, created the Table of Ranks binding the nobility to lifelong service, and had his own son Alexei tortured and killed in 1718 for resisting his project.

The Treaty of Nystad ended the war in 1721 with the Baltic provinces and a sea coast won, and Peter accepted the title Emperor of All Russia, declaring the Tsardom of Muscovy at an end and the Russian Empire in its place.
